title: Inside the Checkpoint: Kannai and the Making of Yokohama
standfirst: A fishing hamlet was chosen over its larger neighbor to keep foreign traders off the shogun's highway, and the guard posts at the bridges into the new port gave the district its name: Kannai, "inside the barrier." Reclaimed twice more, by treaty diplomacy and then by earthquake rubble, this ground still carries street names the eighteen-fifties laid down.

sections.heading: A crossed beach becomes a village

paragraphs.text: Little here is original ground: the Geospatial Information Authority's landform survey reads more than half the study area as former water or sandbar and over half again as artificial fill. A 1913 history of the city traces the name Yokohama itself to this geography, describing a sandbar running northwest from the foot of a hill near today's Motomachi toward what is now a lighthouse-testing station, so that the spit of land lay crosswise, yoko, in the sea. Thirteen households fished here three centuries before the port opened; by the early Edo period the hamlet, once grouped with its neighbors as a single Ishikawa village, had split off as Yokohama-mura in its own right, with 87 households recorded by the account, hemmed by the coast, a tidal inlet, and two sister villages. A map of "Yokohama village and its surroundings" drawn up in 1851 and reproduced in the city's 1933 history shows exactly this: a thin fishing settlement strung along the shore with open water and marsh on every other side, only eight years before it became the center of a treaty port.

sections.heading: A province older than the port

paragraphs.text: The wider region the fishing hamlet belonged to is documented far earlier than the hamlet itself. Gumyoji temple, a few kilometers inland, appears in a document of 1181 as a hereditary house of prayer for the Minamoto clan, and the Yokohama region passed in turn through the hands of Kamakura-period retainers, the Hojo regents, and, once the Ashikaga shogunate installed its own deputies as Kanto Kanrei, the Uesugi houses that served under them; a Hojo clan land register of 1559 still lists named vassals holding fiefs across the wider district by the time Hojo Soun's descendants dominated the whole of the Kanto region. None of this administrative history touched the little fishing settlement directly — Yokohama-mura was a footnote to all of it — until foreign treaties made its obscurity useful.

sections.heading: The swap that named the district

paragraphs.text: The treaties Japan signed with Western powers in 1858 named Kanagawa, the substantial Tokaido post town a few kilometers north, as the port to open the following year. The shogunate had other ideas: an official named Mizuno Chikugo-no-kami, backed by the senior councillor Ii Naosuke, argued for substituting the smaller fishing village of Yokohama across the bay, chiefly to keep foreign residents away from the crowded highway that daimyo processions used. The American consul-general Townsend Harris and his British counterpart, Rutherford Alcock, protested hard: the treaty text said Kanagawa, Yokohama was unnamed and unsuited to trade, and keeping foreigners off the highway seemed to violate the spirit of friendship the treaties claimed. The shogunate answered that Yokohama was technically part of Kanagawa Bay, sat conveniently near Kamakura, Uraga and the scenic spots of Kanazawa and Enoshima, and made a naturally superior harbor — and then set out to prove it, building bridges, a wharf, five new streets, and, at the center of the reclaimed village, a customs house.

That customs house stood at the center of the new port. Officials called Kanagawa Magistrates were installed to handle both foreign and domestic affairs from the middle of 1859, with a separate office at Tobe handling ordinary judicial business while the customs post in the heart of Yokohama village took charge of tariffs and foreign matters. The district's name, though, comes from the port's guard posts: barriers at the bridges into the new town, at Yoshida Bridge and across a newly dug canal, checked everyone who crossed, and the ground inside them became Kannai, "inside the barrier," and everything beyond it Kangai. The tax breaks, reclaimed swampland and subsidized tenements worked: merchants and, eventually, the foreign consulates themselves abandoned their preference for Kanagawa, with the Dutch consulate agreeing to move to Yokohama in January 1861 (the twelfth month of 1860 by the old calendar) and the other powers following despite their own governments' instructions. No single day marks the change formally — historians of the port conventionally use 1 July 1859 (2 June by the old calendar, the date Yokohama still keeps as its official Port Opening Day), technically the date fixed for Kanagawa's own opening — but by the accepted terms of the deal it was Yokohama, not Kanagawa, that became Japan's first great treaty port.

sections.heading: A settlement, and the town beside it called Nankin-machi

paragraphs.text: As building of the foreign settlement began at the waterfront, Yokohama village's own farming families were moved out in 1860 to the foot of the Bluff, in what is now Motomachi, and the district was built up southward in stages, largely complete by about 1863. Chinese residents, drawn first as compradors and laborers for other foreign trading houses, gathered naturally in one part of the new settlement — lots 120 to 160 along what is now Yamashita-cho — well before Japan and China had any treaty of their own; a formal treaty of amity and commerce between the two countries only followed on 13 September 1871. Trade then grew quickly enough that a Qing consulate opened at lot 135 in 1877, and by the years before the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95 the quarter's population had reached 3,000, falling sharply when diplomatic relations broke off — about 500 residents stayed on under Japanese official protection — before recovering once the war ended. From 1899, when the ban on mixed residence was lifted and Japanese could live inside the former settlement, Japanese shopkeepers moved into the district too, and by around 1907 it held some 350 households and 4,000 people; on the eve of the 1923 earthquake, the population is put at about 5,000.

Contemporary Yokohama called the quarter Nankin-machi, after Nanjing and the south Chinese coast most of its early residents came from, rather than the generic "China town" used elsewhere in Japan. An official 1933 account of the city's customs describes its busiest block, along lots 143 to 154, as a row of two-story red-brick shops decorated with gilded and colored carving, with the narrower lanes behind them densely packed with smaller housing — a description of a working immigrant quarter that, more than a century later, both the street plan and the trade have outlasted.

The Great Kanto earthquake struck Kannai hard; the 1933 customs account of Chinatown alone records more than a thousand dead or injured in that one quarter. The recovery took a distinctively Yokohama form: the sea off Yamashita-cho's waterfront was designated a dumping ground for the earthquake's rubble, and between 1925 and 1930 that fill, together with earth from a cliff at Motomachi brought down by the quake and from a road cutting at Uchikoshi, was built up and landscaped into Yamashita Park, opened in 1930 as Japan's first purpose-built waterfront urban park, according to the Agency for Cultural Affairs' own heritage register. What had been open water in the 1859 settlement plan was now solid, public ground.

sections.heading: 1945: burned again, and held by an occupying army

paragraphs.text: On the morning of 29 May 1945, some 517 American B-29 bombers dropped roughly 438,000 incendiary bombs on Yokohama in about an hour; the city's own official figures, issued shortly afterward, record 3,650 dead, 10,198 injured, 309 missing and 311,218 people left homeless, with the fire concentrated on Naka, Minami, Nishi and Kanagawa wards — Naka Ward holding Kannai and Chinatown both. The war's end did not return the district to ordinary life. Occupation forces requisitioned central Yokohama and its port facilities so broadly, the city's own account states, that municipal government almost stopped functioning: offices, department stores, theaters, schools and parks were all taken over, and the outbreak of the Korean War in June 1950 delayed their release still further. Requisitioned land came back only piecemeal over the following decade and a half — the Osanbashi pier in February 1952, Yokohama Park that April, and the housing built on Yamashita Park's own grounds not until June 1960, nearly fifteen years after the surrender.

Of the five streets the shogunate laid out to win its argument over Kanagawa — the waterfront road and the parallel streets behind it — Honcho and Benten-dori still carry the names given them at the 1859 opening, and the 1859 land-division plan reproduced in the city's 1933 history, which its editors judged was largely carried out as drawn, can be laid beside a modern aerial photograph to see how much of that first layout survives. Chinatown's gates stand roughly where lots 120 to 160 once ran, home under the trade association's own count to more than 400 shops and restaurants, on the same footprint an 1871 treaty and a compradors' economy first filled in. Yamashita Park's lawns remain, functionally, the flattened remains of 1923's destruction, and the requisitioned buildings that once stood in for a defeated capital's own damaged offices are gone, but the decade-and-a-half gap between surrender and return is still legible in how late, relative to the rest of Japan, central Yokohama's postwar rebuilding properly began.

timeline.what: Gumyoji temple, the oldest documented place name within today's Yokohama City, appears in a historical record.
The fishing hamlet of Yokohama-mura splits off from Ishikawa village, reaching 87 households.
Treaty negotiations substitute Yokohama for the named treaty port of Kanagawa; a customs house is built at the village's center.
The Dutch consulate agrees to move to Yokohama, and other powers follow despite their governments' preference for Kanagawa.
Yokohama village's farmers are relocated and the foreign settlement is built southward, substantially complete by 1863.
Japan and China sign their first treaty of amity and commerce, formalizing the status of the Chinese residents already settled at Yamashita-cho.
A Qing consulate opens in Nankin-machi at lot 135.
The Great Kanto earthquake devastates Kannai and Chinatown; the city begins dumping rubble into the sea off Yamashita-cho.
Yamashita Park opens on reclaimed earthquake rubble, Japan's first purpose-built waterfront urban park.
The Great Yokohama Air Raid burns Naka, Minami, Nishi and Kanagawa wards; the city records 3,650 dead.
Occupation forces requisition central Yokohama; the last of the Yamashita Park land is not returned until June 1960.

walk.name: The former customs-house site, Nihon-odori
walk.what: The shogunate's customs house stood here, on what is now the Kanagawa Prefectural Office site, with the foreign settlement to its east and the Japanese town to its west; Kannai ("inside the barrier") is named for the guard posts that once stood at the bridges into this port town.

caveats: No single date marks Yokohama's formal replacement of Kanagawa as the treaty port; this dossier follows historians' conventional use of 1 July 1859 (2 June by the old lunisolar calendar, still kept as Yokohama's official Port Opening Day), while noting that this date technically derives from Kanagawa's own designated opening.

Casualty and population figures for Nankin-machi in the 1923 earthquake and interwar period come from the city's own 1933 customs-history volume and are not independently cross-checked against a second source in this session.

Some medieval land-tenure detail drawn from the 1933 Yokohama City history (S2) concerns the wider Yokohama region rather than sites confirmed to lie inside this district's exact study radius, and is used only as general background on the area's depth of settlement.
